original_value: AbstractFor virtually as long as linguists have studied contact‐induced grammatical change, the borrowing of morphological formatives and patterns has been considered a relatively infrequent phenomenon—a view which is reflected in all well‐known borrowability scales. Yet all those scales have been constructed from limited data sets, thus producing rather intuitive generalizations, for example, that inflection is more resistant to borrowing than derivation. In reality, we do not have a precise idea of the global extent of the phenomenon. In particular, the borrowing of compounding techniques is a virtually uninvestigated topic. In recent years, linguists have more intensively pursued a line of research that identifies in the study of contact‐induced change a source of evidence for the theory of grammar and aims to show that different degrees of borrowability reflect fine‐grained distinctions between subcomponents of morphology. The ever‐growing availability of comprehensive grammars and detailed case studies has supplied an adequate empirical basis to reach this goal.

result.paraphrase: Abstract Since linguists first began studying contact-induced grammatical change, the borrowing of morphological formatives and patterns has been regarded as relatively uncommon, a judgment echoed by all major borrowability scales. However, those scales rest on limited datasets and therefore yield somewhat intuitive generalizations, such as the claim that inflection resists borrowing more than derivation. In fact, the global scope of the phenomenon remains unclear. Especially underexplored is the borrowing of compounding techniques, which has received virtually no investigation. In recent years, linguists have more actively developed a research program that treats contact-induced change as evidence for grammatical theory and seeks to demonstrate that differences in borrowability correspond to fine-grained distinctions among morphological subcomponents. The steadily expanding availability of comprehensive grammars and detailed case studies has provided a sufficient empirical foundation for this aim.
